ECHA proposal Annex XV Restriction Report on Lead in Outdoor Shooting and Fishing Comments by WWF Finland and BirdLife Finland

WWF Finland is part of the extensive international WWF network that has offices in about 50 countries and operations in over one hundred countries. In Finland, we have operated since 1972. Our target is to protect the biodiversity of nature and reduce the size of the human ecological footprint. WWF Finland has 68000 financial supporters. BirdLife Finland is the Finnish partner of BirdLife International, the world’s largest nature conservation partnership which strives to conserve birds, their habitats and global biodiversity, working with people towards sustainability in the use of natural resources. BirdLife Finland is the parent organization of 30 regional ornithological societies and has over 22 000 members and supporters.

General comments We write in support of the ECHA proposal Annex XV Restriction Report on Lead in Outdoor Shooting and Fishing. The proposed restriction is based on a large body of evidence of the negative impacts to the health of people, wildlife as well as agricultural animals and soils from lead ammunition and fishing sinkers. The proposed transition periods seem appropriate and will allow plenty of time for hunters, sports shooters, and fishers to find the alternatives suitable for their needs. The Finnish situation We see many responses to the consultation from Finland, which reveal resistance to change to non-lead ammunition. Evidence shows, however, that lead poisoning is a very serious problem also for Finnish wildlife. The risks to Finnish wildlife especially the White-tailed Eagle population are described in scientific publications such as these: Isomursu et al (2018) and Krone et al (2006). The responses from Finland also show that regulatory action is required as voluntary measures will most likely not work. Specific notes on shooting ranges We note that this important study from Finland by Sorvari et al (2006) is missing from the Restriction Report. The abstract is reproduced here: “In Finland, shooting ranges are among the most common activities causing soil contamination. According to our study based on questionnaires and previous regional surveys, the total number of Finnish outdoor shooting ranges is between 2000 and 2500. Most of the ranges are small and only ca. 5% exceed 20 ha. Almost a third of the ranges can cause a groundwater pollution risk, while only few cause an immediate health risk. In the first instance, 50-60 shooting ranges identified as being high-risk areas should be

investigated in detail. At present, the risk management options at Finnish shooting ranges are very limited. Hence, soil excavation combined with disposal is the most common remediation technique. Some of the remediation methods used in other countries have been proven unsuitable in Finnish conditions. Therefore, new, feasible, cost-effective and economical remediation technologies are needed. To exclude future contamination, a total ban of lead shot would be the most effective way.” The paper provides costs calculated at the time for the decontamination of some of the ranges – costed at €250 million. Similarly, the study by Selonen et al (2012) is missing from the main report. Again the abstract is reproduced here which highlights the risks to aquifers from shooting ranges: “Changes in leaching, availability, bioaccumulation, and vertical distribution of lead (Pb) in soil 20 years after the cessation of shooting activity were studied by comparing three pine forest sites in southern Finland: an active shooting range, an abandoned shooting range, and a noncontaminated control site. At both shooting ranges, shooting activity had lasted for 20 years, but it had taken place 20 years earlier at the abandoned range. Up to 4 kg m−2 of Pb pellets had accumulated in the soil at both shooting ranges, and extremely high Pb concentrations, reaching 50,000 mg kg−1, were detected in the organic soil layer. Elevated Pb concentrations were also found in leachate waters and in the biota. Concentrations of Pb in the top organic soil layer and in some of the biota were lower at the abandoned shooting range, which can be taken as a sign of starting recovery of the forest ecosystem. However, the concentration of water-extractable Pb had not decreased in the topsoil, possibly indicating the release of Pb from decaying litter. Deeper in the organic soil layer, weathering of Pb pellets enhanced Pb availability and leaching, indicating an increased risk of groundwater contamination over time at shooting sites located above aquifers.” There are several Finnish responses to the consultation which suggest that leaching of lead from shooting ranges does not occur. This is not true and some of the evidence for this comes from studies of Finnish shooting ranges e.g. Hartikainen and Kerko (2009). Finland is a wet country with acidic soils which increases mobility of lead in soils and via surface water. Aquatic wildlife is sensitive to the effects of lead – including fish which become contaminated as shown by Heier et al (2009) in their study of leachate from a shooting range in Finland. The study by Rantalainen et al (2006) of the distribution of lead from a Finnish shooting range into a wide range of invertebrates provides a concerning picture to indicate how lead from shooting ranges may in effect extent into wider ecosystems when these invertebrates are consumed by vertebrates whether birds, mammals, herptiles or fish. The responses also suggest that somehow the national defence of Finland will be affected by the restriction. That is clearly not the intention. We sincerely hope that derogations for sports shooting will not be made because of the huge weight of lead bullets and gunshot and the nature of much of the environment in Finland. If a derogation is granted for sports shooting with bullets, there must be strict environmental monitoring in particular with respect to water run-off. We question whether monitoring is currently good enough to meet requirements under the EU Water Framework Directive.

Alternatives to lead ammunition We see that ECHA made a request to the Finnish Hunting Association to provide information on some sorts of bullets and some research was undertaken. Findings from this work need to be further elaborated and tests done for lead contamination in the birds shot. Perhaps the important point about the study is that the calibres can be replaced with non-lead alternatives. Allowing some lead bullets with special construction and potentially lower fragmentation (although further research needed) risks undermining the wider restriction and creating the problems of partial restriction. Conclusion We strongly support the proposed restriction on lead ammunition and fishing sinkers.

Jari Luukkonen, conservation director, WWF Finland

Aki Arkiomaa, director, BirdLife Finland
